summary: This work systematically identifies and quantitatively models two dominant microwave crosstalk mechanisms in planar superconducting quantum devices: proximity-induced crosstalk from drive lines routed near qubits, and crossover-induced crosstalk from drive lines crossing qubit-qubit couplers via air bridges. Electrostatic and RF finite-element simulations combined with experimental measurements on test structures and a 17-qubit processor establish predictive models showing that package-mediated coupling decays as $-2.7$ dB/mm (much slower than direct capacitance at $-26$ dB/mm), imposing stringent layout constraints on scaling.
motivation: Microwave crosstalk introduces control errors and becomes increasingly severe in scaled superconducting quantum processors due to frequency crowding and proliferating parasitic coupling pathways, yet quantitative physical models accounting for on-chip circuit elements remain underdeveloped.
method: Test devices with tunable qubit separations ($d \in \{550, 738, 947, 1165\}$ μm) and varying air-bridge geometries ($C_{\text{cross}} \in \{1.1, 2.2\}$ fF) were fabricated in 120 nm niobium on high-resistivity silicon and characterized by measuring cross-drive ratios $X_{k,j} = (\Omega_{k,j}/\Omega_{j,j})^2$ via Rabi oscillations. Crosstalk was modeled by combining direct capacitive coupling with package-volume effects through standing-wave analysis and RF simulations.
result: Measured crosstalk agreed quantitatively with models treating both capacitive and package-mediated mechanisms (e.g., Fig. 3b); proximity-induced crosstalk alone underestimated observed effects by factors up to $3\times$ at large distances. Reducing air-bridge cross-capacitance from $2.2$ fF to $0.6$ fF yields $11$ dB crosstalk reduction; achieving $10^{-4}$ single-qubit error at zero detuning requires $X < -42$ dB or alternatively $\Delta_{dq}/2\pi > 80$ MHz detuning when $X = -10$ dB.
